item.title: Closed-loop photoreactor design enabled by machine learning and digital twins
item.dc:creator: Jasper H. A. Schuurmans
Miguel Claros
Elia Savino
Florian Lukas
Aidan Slattery
Timothy Noël
item.description:
Authors: Jasper H. A. Schuurmans, Miguel Claros, Elia Savino, Florian Lukas, Aidan Slattery, Timothy Noël
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Designing efficient photoreactors remains challenging due to the complex interplay of reflection, scattering, and absorption. Here, we introduce a closed-loop workflow integrating ray-tracing digital twins with multi-objective Bayesian optimization to design photoreactors with high photon capture and uniform irradiation. A digital 3D reactor model is calibrated using measured emission characteristics, reflectivity data, and geometrical properties and validated against potassium ferrioxalate actinometry. The validated model explores reflector shape and vial positioning, identifying geometries that maximize incident photon flux while maintaining homogeneity across 16 vials. Experimental validation using a photocatalytic Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling shows that reaction yields track simulated photon flux. The optimized reactor is further applied to quantum-yield screening, enabling mechanistic insights across diverse conditions in a single experiment. This work establishes an experimentally validated virtual co-design framework in which machine learning and digital twins accelerate photoreactor development and support quantitative understanding of photochemical processes.

item.title: Nuclear adaptation to intracellular mechanical forces regulates the phagocytic capacity of Drosophila macrophages in vivo
item.dc:creator: Clelia Amato
Rosina Graham
Rosalind Heron
Sebastian Rogatti
Christopher J. Anderson
Stephen J. Jenkins
Will Wood
item.description:
Authors: Clelia Amato, Rosina Graham, Rosalind Heron, Sebastian Rogatti, Christopher J. Anderson, Stephen J. Jenkins, Will Wood
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract How macrophages fine-tune their appetite to fulfil their clearance role is incompletely understood. Phagocytosis exacerbates cytoplasmic crowding, but whether macrophages can sense this increase and use it to regulate their phagocytic capacity has never been investigated. Here, we test the hypothesis that phagosomes exert a strain on the nucleus, which in turn responds to the intracellular mechanical inputs influencing macrophage appetite. Combining genetic manipulation and live in vivo imaging, we show that engulfed apoptotic bodies indent and deform the nucleus of Drosophila embryonic macrophages, and that phagocytosis increases Lamin B levels. Importantly, we show that silencing Lamin B or components of the LINC complex negatively regulates apoptotic body engulfment in vivo. Thus, we demonstrate that phagosome-induced nuclear molecular and mechanical adaptations are critical for Drosophila embryonic macrophages to sustain apoptotic corpse uptake, thereby unveiling a role for nuclear plasticity in the regulation of macrophage phagocytic capacity in vivo.

item.title: Superradiant charge density waves in a driven hybrid cavity-matter system
item.dc:creator: Luka Skolc
Sambuddha Chattopadhyay
Filip Marijanović
Qitong Li
Jonathan Keeling
Benjamin L. Lev
Eugene Demler
item.description:
Authors: Luka Skolc, Sambuddha Chattopadhyay, Filip Marijanović, Qitong Li, Jonathan Keeling, Benjamin L. Lev, Eugene Demler
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Optical cavities enable strong, long-range, light-matter interactions that drive collective ordering, such as superradiant self-organization in ultracold atomic gases. Extending these ideas to solid-state electron systems could enable continuous-wave optical control of electronic order, but is impeded by the mismatch between optical wavelengths and electronic length scales. Here, we propose a platform for realizing superradiant charge density waves in doped, driven transition-metal dichalcogenides coupled to an optical cavity. A nanoscale grating generates electric fields at large in-plane optical momenta, allowing cavity photons to couple efficiently to electronic density fluctuations through exciton-polaron processes. Using a linear-stability analysis, we determine the threshold for superradiant ordering and map out the driven phase diagram. We show that matching the grating periodicity to the enhanced electronic density fluctuations—such as those near Wigner crystallization—lowers the required pump intensity. Our results establish a route toward cavity-controlled electronic order in quantum materials.

item.title: Transforming electrified railway into mechanical energy storage for electricity system decarbonization
item.dc:creator: Can Wan
Xitong Mu
Zihan He
Hui Liu
Pierre Pinson
Ping Ju
Qianwen Xu
item.description:
Authors: Can Wan, Xitong Mu, Zihan He, Hui Liu, Pierre Pinson, Ping Ju, Qianwen Xu
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Decarbonizing electricity requires vast energy storage capacity worldwide, but constructing dedicated storage assets creates substantial capital, material and embodied carbon burdens. Electrified railways already exchange energy with electricity systems through traction and regenerative braking, but their inherent potential as mechanical energy storage remains unexploited. Here we show that modulation of train operations can transform electrified railways into Electrified Rail-Based Energy Storage. By analyzing 326,034 inter-stop train operations, we estimate its global potential at 190 gigawatts in 2025 and 315–579 gigawatts by 2050. Capacity expansion models for China, Europe and India indicate that it can reduce investment in conventional storage by 11.9–20.0%, corresponding to an extrapolated global value of US$14.9–35.1 billion annually. Without increasing total system cost, electricity systems with this flexible resource could further reduce operational CO 2 emissions by 94.3–258.9 million tonnes per year. Electrified railways can therefore complement conventional storage technologies for electricity system decarbonization.

item.title: Resolving short-term meteorological variability amplifies projected glacier loss and sea-level rise
item.dc:creator: Lander Van Tricht
Matthias Huss
Harry Zekollari
Rodrigo Aguayo
Janosch Beer
Marit van Tiel
Alexandra von der Esch
Daniel Farinotti
item.description:
Authors: Lander Van Tricht, Matthias Huss, Harry Zekollari, Rodrigo Aguayo, Janosch Beer, Marit van Tiel, Alexandra von der Esch, Daniel Farinotti
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10696
Abstract: Abstract Global glacier models typically rely on temperature-index mass balance calculations forced with aggregated meteorological data, limiting their ability to resolve short-term variability. Here, we develop a daily-resolution version of the Global Glacier Evolution Model (GloGEM), which we apply globally and compare against the monthly configuration. Our results show that the daily model more closely reproduces mass balance observations and provides a more detailed representation of glacier runoff. Accounting for short-term meteorological variability leads to systematically greater projected mass loss, with up to 25% greater loss in Svalbard. These differences arise from extreme melt days, precipitation-phase transitions, and surface-type feedbacks not fully represented at monthly resolution. Globally, the daily model yields ice volume losses of 26 ± 10% under low-emission and 47 ± 17% under high-emission scenarios over 2025-2100 (ensemble mean ± 1 StD), resulting in an additional 5-10% mass loss (20-33 mm of global mean sea-level rise) relative to the monthly implementation. Resolving high-frequency forcing, or accounting for its effects through parameterisations, is therefore essential for robust glacier projections, while its omission may systematically underestimate future glacier loss.

item.title: Controlling the shell growth mechanism and interfacial oxidation of InAs/ZnSe quantum dots for shortwave infrared emission
item.dc:creator: Taewan Kim
Manuela De Franco
Miguel Dosil
Jae Taek Oh
Rajesh Bera
Marta Martos Valverde
Gaurav Kumar
Gerasimos Konstantatos
item.description:
Authors: Taewan Kim, Manuela De Franco, Miguel Dosil, Jae Taek Oh, Rajesh Bera, Marta Martos Valverde, Gaurav Kumar, Gerasimos Konstantatos
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 9969
Abstract: Abstract Short-wave infrared (SWIR) emitters underpin applications in communication, imaging and sensing, yet efficient, scalable devices remain limited. Colloidal InAs quantum dots (InAs CQDs) offer a compelling, cost-effective alternative to conventional epitaxial SWIR light-emitting diodes (LEDs). However, developing heavy-metal-free InAs CQDs for emission beyond 1400 nm is hindered by lattice mismatch during core/shell growth, which degrades photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY). Furthermore, integrating CQDs into LEDs often introduces severe interfacial quenching and intrinsic charge imbalances. Here we report a highly efficient heavy-metal-free SWIR LED operating at 1525 nm, enabled by tailored injection strategies and oxidation-induced interfacial engineering. Optimized high-temperature ZnCl₂ treatment and continuous precursor injection improve shell nucleation and growth, while controlled interfacial oxidation is associated with reduced shell-thickness-dependent strain signatures and improved PLQY retention during shell thickening. Together, these strategies yield measured PLQYs exceeding 55% for emission beyond 1400 nm. Moreover, we demonstrate that incorporating a semiconducting InAs CQD interlayer effectively suppresses interfacial quenching and regulates electron over-injection. Combined with a doped hole-transport layer to reduce series resistance, our optimized devices achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency of 3.5% and a record radiance of ~17 W sr −1 m −2 , alongside a T50 operational lifetime of 16 h. Our findings suggest that integrating mechanism-driven shell growth with rational device engineering offers a strategy to overcome current bottlenecks in colloidal emitters, facilitating the transition toward short-wave infrared applications.

item.title: Plasma eMTBR-tau243 and p-tau205 as T2 biomarkers for biological staging and prognosis in Alzheimer’s disease
item.dc:creator: Sohyun Yim
Eun Hye Lee
Jungah Lee
Daeun Shin
Heekyoung Kang

item.description:
Authors: Sohyun Yim, Eun Hye Lee, Jungah Lee, Daeun Shin, Heekyoung Kang, Hee Kyung Park, Seonghyeon Kim, Joel B. Braunstein, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Plasma biomarkers that reflect distinct stages of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) could enable scalable biological staging. We evaluated phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species across multiple analytical platforms and the endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region containing residue 243 (eMTBR-tau243) using a dedicated LC-MS/MS platform in a well-characterized cohort with amyloid PET and a subset with tau PET. While T1 biomarkers increased during preclinical stages, eMTBR-tau243 and p-tau205 increased later, consistent with fibrillar tau aggregation. eMTBR-tau243 showed the strongest and stage-dependent associations with regional tau PET and cognition, outperforming T1 biomarkers in predicting cross-sectional and longitudinal cognition. A plasma-based tau staging system integrating p-tau217 and eMTBR-tau243 closely aligned with PET-based tau staging and predicted longitudinal cognitive trajectories. These findings support plasma eMTBR-tau243 as a prototypical T2 biomarker and highlight the potential of plasma-based tau staging for prognosis and therapeutic decision-making in AD.

item.title: Rapid assessment of chemical complementarity of ligands for protein design
item.dc:creator: Rokas Petrenas

Joel J. Chubb

item.description:
Authors: Rokas Petrenas, Katarzyna Ożga, Joel J. Chubb, Andrey V. Romanyuk, Dominic Alibhai, Jennifer J. McManus, Graham J. Leggett, Nigel S. Scrutton, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Driven by deep-learning methods, computational protein design can now rapidly generate de novo structures, opening new frontiers for creating proteins that bind small molecules tightly and specifically, although achieving predictable and tunable binding remains challenging. Here we address this with a rapid physics-based computational method to generate isosteric and chemically complementary binding pockets for small-molecule targets in de novo designed proteins. We test this experimentally by constructing and characterizing binding proteins for several synthetic and natural chromophores. By evaluating only single-digit numbers of designs, the pipeline delivers stable proteins with pre-organised binding sites in apo structures confirmed by X-ray crystallography, which bind the targets with micromolar affinities or better. To illustrate the scope and applications of this approach, we incorporate selective and coupled chromophore-binding sites in a two-domain de novo protein enabling controlled energy transfer between the two sites, and we develop a small de novo binding protein that can be used in live mammalian cells to visualise sub-cellular structures.

item.title: Near-infrared-responsive thia-hexaphyrin-based covalent organic frameworks for cancer phototherapy
item.dc:creator: Yu Xiao
Ziyue Huang
Shihuai Wang
Xiaoyi Xu

Jingjing Guo

Yang Liu
item.description:
Authors: Yu Xiao, Ziyue Huang, Shihuai Wang, Xiaoyi Xu, Yu Cheng, Jingjing Guo, Ting He, Yang Liu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Covalent organic frameworks (COF) have emerged as promising phototherapeutic platforms for tumor therapy, where the columnar π-arrayed metal-free photosensitizers serve as both a cooperative light-harvesting antenna and a semiconducting scaffold for efficient charge-carrier separation and transport. However, the phototherapeutic agents based on COFs are usually activated with ultraviolet and visible light, resulting in the limitation of deep-tissue phototherapy. Herein, we develop near-infrared-responsive COFs through elaborate design and synthesis of a thia-hexaphyrin building block, which feature well-aligned conjugation skeletons for the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and photothermal effect upon 808 nm laser irradiation, outperforming conventional porphyrin-based COFs. This porous framework exhibits high phototherapeutic efficacy, leading to the tumor suppression for 4T1 tumors and CT26 tumors in female mouse model by inducing immunogenic cell death through phototherapy and triggering systemic anti-tumor immune responses.

item.title: Passive abortive infection mechanisms targeting phage long tail fiber proteins
item.dc:creator: Jie Cheng
Hongfan Zhai
Rui Sun
Ting Liu
Qiang Chen
Yamei Yu
item.description:
Authors: Jie Cheng, Hongfan Zhai, Rui Sun, Ting Liu, Qiang Chen, Yamei Yu
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Bacteria employ diverse defense strategies against phage infection, yet mechanisms directly targeting viral proteins remain scarcely documented. In this study, we characterize two bacterial defense systems: TFAD1 featuring a serine protease and TFAD2 featuring a Ser/Thr kinase. We show that TFAD1 and TFAD2 act on phage long tail fiber proteins via protein degradation and phosphorylation, respectively. Intriguingly, both systems allow complete phage replication cycles but generate non-infective progeny—a mechanism distinct from classical abortive infection (Abi), which we term “passive Abi”. Our findings expand the paradigm of bacterial immunity by unveiling protease- and kinase-mediated incapacitation of phage structural proteins, offering insights into the molecular arms race between bacteria and phages.

item.title: Projected intensification of soil salinization in global drylands under future aridity increase
item.dc:creator: Dietian Yu
Nan Wang
Amirhossein Hassani
Saverio Perri
Yi Peng
Songchao Chen
Jie Peng
Yulin Shangguan
item.description:
Authors: Dietian Yu, Nan Wang, Amirhossein Hassani, Saverio Perri, Yi Peng, Songchao Chen, Jie Peng, Yulin Shangguan, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Soil salinization threatens agricultural production, water management, and ecosystem health. Yet, how increasing aridity will reshape 21st-century soil salinity patterns across drylands, particularly in croplands, remains unclear. Here, we compile a relatively comprehensive global soil salinity dataset from the past two decades, projecting future dryland soil salinity dynamics using climate-driven machine learning models with multiple covariates, including dynamic dryland extent and human influences. Our results show an 8% expansion of global drylands saline soils under increasing aridity by 2100 (SSP5-8.5) relative to 2004–2023. Southwestern US, Mexico, southern Europe, central South America, eastern and southern Africa are highest-risk hotspots. We further show dryland croplands face serious salinization, especially irrigated systems, where half of these newly salinized areas project more than 4.9% (maize), 17.2% (dryland rice), 3.3% (sorghum), and 21.2% (wheat) potential production losses. Our findings inform long-term adaptation strategies to mitigate emerging salinization risks and sustain water and food security.

item.dc:creator: Rong Guo
Kenneisha Norford
Ling Xu

Stephanie Halene

item.description:
Authors: Rong Guo, Kenneisha Norford, Ling Xu, Manyi Wei, Wenshuai Wang, Stephanie Halene, Anna Marie Pyle
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10366
Abstract: Abstract Retinoic acid-inducible gene-I (RIG-I) plays a pivotal role in recognizing and combating RNA viruses in humans, and it has become a drug target of significant interest. RIG-I agonists composed of dsRNA represent antiviral and antitumor therapies, however the development of small-molecule RIG-I agonists, with their potential for improved pharmacokinetics, remains an unmet need. Here, we report small-molecule RIG-I agonists that directly activate the RIG-I receptor protein. These agonists stimulate the first step in RIG-I signaling by triggering release of the signaling domains (CARDs) from an autorepressed form of the protein. This was achieved by developing a sensitive high-throughput screening (HTS) assay that directly monitors CARD expulsion through optical methods. The resulting screen hits were refined and optimized, leading to a specific RIG-I agonist that induces a robust interferon response. This study establishes a pharmacophore and assay for development of small molecules that precisely modulate RIG-I signaling.

item.title: Molecular architecture of Cryptococcus cell walls reveals species-specific chitosan-dependent remodeling
item.dc:creator: Ankur Ankur
Rajendra Upadhya
Mahsa Doosti
Davis Ferreira
Sara E. Miller
Li Xie
Ivan Hung
Jennifer K. Lodge
item.description:
Authors: Ankur Ankur, Rajendra Upadhya, Mahsa Doosti, Davis Ferreira, Sara E. Miller, Li Xie, Ivan Hung, Jennifer K. Lodge, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii are fungal pathogens that cause life-threatening infections, including cryptococcal meningitis. A distinctive feature of the cryptococcal cell wall is the extensive deacetylation of chitin to chitosan, a modification that is essential for virulence but whose structural role in cell-wall organization remains poorly understood. Here, we analyze the cell walls of wild-type strains of both species and their avirulent chitosan-deficient mutants, which serve as vaccine candidates. Loss of chitosan disrupted cell morphology and altered cell-wall ultrastructure, with more pronounced defects in C. neoformans . Solid-state NMR reveals that aggregated α-(1→3)-glucans form the principal rigid domain of the cell wall in both species and are closely associated with chitin microfibrils, whereas surrounding β-glucans and mannoproteins constitute a more dynamic matrix. Chitosan modulates hydration and flexibility, and its loss increases chitin exposure and triggers species-specific remodeling of the polysaccharide network. In C. neoformans , chitosan depletion increased α-(1→3)-glucan content and reduced β-glucan levels, whereas C. gattii selectively lost one α-(1→3)-glucan subtype while maintaining β-glucan levels. Although capsule production remained intact, chitosan deficiency altered glucuronoxylomannan linkage patterns and mannoprotein composition. These findings reveal how chitosan organizes cryptococcal cell-wall architecture and highlight distinct structural adaptation strategies among pathogenic Cryptococcus species.

item.title: Solvent heterogeneity regulates assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization
item.dc:creator: Goutam Ghosh
Jim Bachmann
Marvin Nyenhuis
Timo Krüger
Zulema Fernández
João Paulo Coelho
Antonia Albers
Max Köyer
item.description:
Authors: Goutam Ghosh, Jim Bachmann, Marvin Nyenhuis, Timo Krüger, Zulema Fernández, João Paulo Coelho, Antonia Albers, Max Köyer, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Supramolecular polymers are fundamental mimics of biological assemblies with diverse functions. However, predicting monomer solubility and controlling the colloidal stability of the resulting assemblies in solution remain major challenges. As a result, their preparation commonly relies on solvent mixtures, which can generate local heterogeneities during sample processing—an effect that remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that solvent heterogeneity biases assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization, with the extent of this effect modulated by monomer structure. Using an amphiphilic Pd(II) complex as a model system, we uncover a thermally accelerated transition from kinetically controlled discrete nanostructures to thermodynamically stable supramolecular polymers in water/1,4-dioxane mixtures. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that this transformation is mediated by microscopic liquid–liquid phase separation within the mixed solvent, creating 1,4-dioxane-enriched microdomains with increased local monomer concentration. Thermal annealing enhances molecular mobility and promotes the growth and coalescence of these microdomains, facilitating the transition to one-dimensional fibers. Extending the investigation to structurally related monomers further identifies the metal center and hydrogen-bonding motifs as key design elements governing this behavior. By linking molecular design and solvent heterogeneity to pathway complexity, our findings highlight how mixed solvents can be used to control supramolecular polymerization.

item.title: Bacteroides–Escherichia interactions contribute to colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile
item.dc:creator: Achuthan Ambat
Naomi Iris van den Berg
Francisco Zorrilla
Shruti Menon
Abhijit Maji
Tanim Islam
Arianna Basile

item.description:
Authors: Achuthan Ambat, Naomi Iris van den Berg, Francisco Zorrilla, Shruti Menon, Abhijit Maji, Tanim Islam, Arianna Basile, Sudeep Ghimire, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Commensal gut bacteria are key contributors to the resilience against pathogen invasion. This is exemplified by the success of faecal microbiota transplantation in treating recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. Yet, characteristics of communities that can confer colonisation resistance and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here we use a synthetic community of 14 commensal gut bacteria to uncover inter-species interactions and metabolic pathways underpinning the emergent resilience against C. difficile invasion. We challenged this synthetic community as well as faecal-matter-derived communities with antibiotic treatment and C. difficile in a continuous flow bioreactor. Using generalised Lotka-Volterra and genome-scale metabolic modelling, we identified interactions between Escherichia coli and Bacteroides/Phocaeicola sp. as key to the pathogen’s suppression. Metabolomics and targeted validation experiments revealed that fructan-derived fructooligosaccharides, vitamin B3 biosynthesis, and competition for Stickland metabolism precursors causally contribute to suppression across multiple C. difficile strains and donor backgrounds. Analysis of metagenomics data from patient cohorts and clinical trials attested the in vivo relevance of the identified metabolic pathways and the ratio between Bacteroides and Escherichia in successful colonisation resistance. The latter was found to be a stronger discriminator than commonly used alpha diversity metrics. Together, our study uncovers emergent microbial interactions in pathogen resistance with implications for rational design of bacteriotherapies.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Loss of transparency due to water vapor condensation is a widespread problem across diverse applications such as windows, eyewear, displays, vehicles, and kitchenware. Facile fabrication and superior performance establish our microstructured hydrogel as an excellent choice for sustaining transparency under extreme condensation.

Abstract: Abstract WHO-endorsed shortened, all-oral regimens have improved tolerability and outcomes for MDR/RR-TB treatment, but predictors of poor outcomes remain incompletely-characterized. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Achieving high energy density without compromising safety remains a significant challenge for advanced batteries. Nonflammable electrolytes can mitigate fire risk, but poor bulk and interfacial properties of such electrolytes limit their application. Here, a nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate electrolyte was developed, achieving a self-extinguishing time of ~0 s and stable cycling in both lithium metal and lithium-ion batteries under high-voltage conditions. These findings suggest that preemptive passivation on both electrodes, when coupled with nonflammable electrolyte design, can provide a viable route toward safe, high-energy lithium batteries.

item.description:
Authors: Shane A. Fiorenza, Sheba Cheeran, Elena Doria, Iva M. Tolić, Patrick Meraldi, Nenad Pavin
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The mitotic spindle is a biomechanical structure whose length must be precisely controlled to ensure faithful chromosome segregation. The treadmilling of microtubules towards spindle poles, termed poleward flux, is involved in spindle length control. However, poleward flux velocity has been shown to be both inversely and directly proportional to spindle length, a contradiction that remains unexplained by current mechanisms. Moreover, our model predicts that spindle length and poleward flux velocity can vary independently via simultaneous perturbations at both microtubule ends, which we validate with protein depletion experiments in human cells. Finally, we provide experimental evidence for length-dependent accumulation of proteins at microtubule minus-ends. Our results thus resolve a longstanding paradox and provide mechanistic insight into the reciprocal control of spindle length and poleward flux.

Abstract: Abstract Many biologically important molecules are structural isomers that share the same molecular mass yet differ in shape, bonding and function. This creates an ambiguity for mass spectrometry imaging (MSI), where chemically distinct species can be indistinguishable on the mass-to-charge ( m/z) scale and therefore cannot be reliably mapped in heterogeneous materials. We benchmark these measurements against ion mobility spectrometry and observe consistent trends between OrbiSIMS transmission behaviour and ion mobility separation. These results establish OrbiSIMS as an approach for isomer-resolved MSI at surfaces and interfaces, opening opportunities to map isomeric biomolecules in complex systems where spatial distribution is central to function.

Abstract: Abstract Mass spectrometry-based proteomics with data-independent acquisition benefits from advanced instrumentation and computational analysis. The method offers a natural treatment of missing values, weighting the imputed values according to the quality metrics in the run. We demonstrate the accuracy of the resulting differential analysis in five experiments: two custom benchmarking studies with intentionally induced anomalies, a controlled mixture of proteomes, and two large-scale clinical investigations. Abstract: Abstract Hydration critically governs the physicochemical behavior of solutes in both the aqueous bulk and interfacial environments. As typical chaotropic Hofmeister ions, weakly hydrated anions (WHAs) can reshape hydration structures and accumulate at water–hydrophobe interfaces. These synergistic effects yield hollow-ridged polyamide selective layers with reduced thickness and high crosslinking density, delivering enhanced water permeance and salt rejection. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Carbon removal and storage is central to many net-zero commitments, yet its durability, particularly for nature-based methods, is uncertain due to disturbance risks. Previous work shows that carbon storage-years (the time-integrated quantity of carbon storage) are proportional to time-integrated avoided warming, which in turn causes avoided changes in slow-responding climate variables. Here, we show that temporary carbon storage results in avoided changes in inertial climate variables. Avoided changes in 2100 are proportional to carbon storage-years across a range of storage amounts and emissions scenarios for permafrost carbon, ocean carbon, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, ocean temperature, and thermosteric sea-level rise. By 2300, proportionality persists in some variables, notably sea-level rise, ocean temperature, and ocean carbon. Temporary storage therefore has climate benefits that extend beyond the duration of the storage, with some persistence of benefits even on multi-century timescales. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

Abstract: Abstract The HIV-1 capsid, composed of capsid (CA) proteins arranged into a conical surface lattice, serves as a critical platform for host–pathogen interactions. Many host cofactors regulate HIV-1 infection by selectively recognizing the higher-order CA lattice rather than individual monomers or capsomers. Among these, Myxovirus resistance protein B (MxB) is a key cellular restriction factor that binds the capsid via its N-terminal fragment containing an arginine-rich motif (RRR), blocking HIV-1 infection at early infection stages. However, the structural basis of this interaction has remained elusive. Notably, residues 10-20 of the MxB N-terminus adopt an α-helical conformation that stabilizes binding at the CA trimer interface, revealing a distinct mode of capsid engagement. These findings provide insight into arginine-rich motif–mediated recognition by MxB and other host factors and establish a structural framework for the development of capsid-targeting antiviral therapeutics.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10876
Abstract: Abstract Despite significant climate variability in the Northern Hemisphere ~50,000–12,000 years ago, the potential for vertebrates to periodically thrive in the glacial Arctic Ocean has been largely overlooked because ecosystem productivity was assumed to be too low. Here, we analyze fish otoliths preserved in deep-sea sediments and find that two Arctic endemic cod species, ice cod ( Arctogadus glacialis ) and polar cod ( Boreogadus saida ), lived at 87–89 °N ~ 48,000–35,000 years ago and reappeared at the onset of the Holocene ~12,000 years ago. These findings suggest that the glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but rather a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish.

Abstract: Abstract Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) remains a major unmet clinical challenge. ANGPTL2 inhibition preserves macrophage intercellular communication and prevents HFpEF development. These findings identify cardiac macrophage signaling rewiring as a central mechanism linking hypertensive stress to metabolic remodeling and inflammation, revealing a pathogenic pathway for HFpEF in the absence of obesity that is distinct from HFpEF associated with obesity.

Abstract: Abstract Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Abstract: Abstract The microRNA-200 family (miR-200s) is known for inhibiting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and cell-cycle progression in cancer, but its function in epithelial development remains unclear. Here we show that miR-200s are highly enriched in hair matrix progenitors but absent from the upper hair follicle (HF), where sebaceous gland (SG) and HF stem cells are specified. Ectopic miR-200 induction abolishes SG specification while preserving hair morphogenesis. Genome-wide identification of miR-200 targets reveals direct repression of negative regulators of WNT signaling and cell-cycle regulators. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses uncover mutually exclusive domains of WNT activity and SOX9 expression in the upper HF that is disrupted by miR-200 induction. Genome-wide mapping of SOX9 targets further uncovers a lipogenic and fatty-acid metabolic program required for SG specification. Together, these findings show that miR-200 blocks SG fate by inhibiting SOX9 function and restricting cell proliferation, defining a spatially organized regulatory network essential for SG development.
